transcriptLines.text: Your heart is a muscle about the size of your fist, and it beats around one hundred thousand times a day.
It sits in the middle of your chest, tilted slightly to the left, protected by the rib cage.
The heart has four chambers. The two upper chambers are called the atria.
The two lower chambers are the ventricles, and they do most of the pumping.
Blood that has delivered its oxygen to the body comes back through two big veins, the venae cavae.
It enters the right atrium, then passes through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle.
The right ventricle pumps that blood through the pulmonary artery to the lungs.
In the lungs the blood drops off carbon dioxide and picks up fresh oxygen.
Oxygen rich blood returns through the pulmonary veins into the left atrium.
From there it flows through the mitral valve into the left ventricle.
The left ventricle has the thickest wall of any chamber, because it pumps blood to the entire body.
It pushes blood through the aortic valve into the aorta, the largest artery in the body.
Valves act like one way doors. The lub dub sound you hear is those valves snapping shut.
The heart muscle itself gets blood from the coronary arteries that wrap around its surface.
A blockage in a coronary artery starves part of the muscle of oxygen, which is a heart attack.
The heartbeat starts in a small cluster of cells called the sinoatrial node, the natural pacemaker.
That electrical signal spreads across the atria, pauses at the atrioventricular node, then races down to the ventricles.
That pause gives the atria time to finish filling the ventricles before they squeeze.
